memoryText: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Matthew 22:37 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
A lawyer tried to test Jesus with a question: which commandment in the law is the greatest? Jesus quoted the Shema from Deuteronomy 6, the words every Jewish child learned.

“You shall love.” The center of the law is love. Love is a command, which means it is a settled direction of the will as well as a feeling. We are commanded because love is owed, and because God knows our hearts will wander if left alone.

“The Lord your God.” The object of love is the Lord, and he is our God, in covenant relationship. He is not an idea or a force. He is a person who has made himself known and who loves us first.

“With all your heart.” The heart in Hebrew thought is the center of the person, including will and desire. To love with all the heart is to desire God above all.

“And with all your soul.” The soul is the whole life. To love with all the soul is to give our lives and energy to him.

“And with all your mind.” The mind is our thinking and understanding. Christianity is not anti-intellectual. We are meant to think about God and his word, and to love him with our minds.

The whole person is to be engaged. Nothing is left over. This is the great and first commandment, and Jesus says that the second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. No one has ever fully kept it except Jesus. He loved the Father perfectly and loved us to the cross. Say this verse each morning and ask him to grow your love.
weekInReview: This week you walked with Jesus toward Jerusalem and into Holy Week. You heard his teaching on marriage, children, and wealth, and saw the rich young man walk away. You learned that greatness in the kingdom means serving, since the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many. You watched the king enter Jerusalem on a donkey, clean out the temple, and tell parables about wicked tenants and a wedding feast. You heard the two great commandments and the seven woes. In the Olivet Discourse, he called you to be ready: like the wise virgins, faithful servants, and those who serve the least of these. Psalm 118 gave you the words the crowds sang and Jesus likely sang that final night. At the Last Supper, he gave you his body and blood of the new covenant, and in Gethsemane he prayed, “Not as I will, but as you will.”
reflectionQuestions: Jesus summed up the law in two commandments: love God and love neighbor. Which of the two do you find harder right now, and why?
In the parable of the sheep and goats, the righteous served Christ without realizing it. Who are “the least of these” near you, and what is one concrete way to serve them?
At the Last Supper, Jesus said his blood is poured out “for the forgiveness of sins.” What does it mean to you personally that he drank the cup of judgment for you?
prayerPrompts: Ask Jesus to help you love God with all your heart and your neighbor as yourself.
Thank him for the cup he drank for you.
